rail_guard.text: Plymouth! Change here for Cornwall, the Navy, and a view of the Sound if you lean out of the window, which you must not.
Brunel's bridge over the Tamar is just up the line. Opened 1859, still carrying trains. Hop on, my lover.

then.text: {greeting} If you hear a drum out in the Sound one night, it's either Drake or the Navy band practising. Either way, very patriotic.
The game finished, the beacons lit, Exeter warned. They'd have had the news inland by morning, fire to fire, hill to hill.
Here. This is a copy of Drake's Drum. They say he took the real one round the world, and that if England's ever in danger, you beat it and he'll come back up the Sound.
And this little one turned up in the Hoe beacon's ashes, warming its toes. It's taken a shine to you.
Now, the tide's on the turn. Time to beat the Spaniards. Or have a cream tea. Same thing, really.
Game won! Now the beacon. The Beacon Warden's up by the Armada Memorial with the matches. Light it, then carry the word up to Haldon Hill and on to Exeter.
The Bowls Captain's waiting on the green. Roll that wood gently, it's got bias.

else.text: {greeting} Sir Francis Drake, at your service. Well, Derek, at your service, but I do the voice at weekends.
Summer of 1588. A ship comes in: the Spanish Armada's off the Lizard! And Drake says: there's time to finish the game, and beat the Spaniards after.
Truth is, the tide was running in and the wind was against them. He couldn't have got the fleet out of the Sound till the evening if he'd tried. So he bowled.
I'm re-enacting it for the visitors and my opponent's very good. Too good. Finish the game for me? Then we light the beacons and send the warning up the country, like they did.

then.text: Champion! The Bowls Captain's on the green with the woods. Mind the jack, it's older than you.

else.text: No hurry. The Armada's been coming for four hundred years, it'll keep.

then.text: A fine game. Bowls is the second oldest thing on the Hoe, after the arguments about it.
So, you're finishing Drake's game? Right. A wood has a bias, it curls in as it slows. Like my temper. Let's see you draw to the jack.
Touched the jack! Off you go, then. The Armada won't beat itself.

else.text: Lawn bowls on Plymouth Hoe. There's been a green up here since before Drake. Mind your feet on the grass, it's been rolled flatter than my pastry.

then.text: She's burning lovely. On a clear night they'd have seen this from Rame Head, Staddon Heights, and up on the edge of Dartmoor.
Bowls finished? Then it's time. In 1588 there were watchmen at beacons all along the coast, with orders to light up the moment they saw the fleet.
You touch the torch to the pitch and tar in the iron basket. It catches with a roar and a great gout of smoke rolls over the Sound.
There she goes! Now the next fire. Haldon Hill, east, past Dartmoor on the way to Exeter. Off you go, quick as you like.

else.text: This is the Hoe beacon. We light it for coronations, jubilees and anniversaries. Last time, a gull tried to sit in it. Once.

then.text: The display's up by the Steps now, with your notes in it. People read it while eating ice creams, which is the highest honour in Plymouth.
Life in a merchant's house, the last night ashore, and the leaky Speedwell. That's the story, all right.
They sailed on the sixth of September 1620. Sixty-six days at sea. A young man died on the way and a baby was born, named Oceanus. You'd remember that name.
Here, for your trouble: some bits from the beach and a flask for the road.
Three things for the display: the Elizabethan House on New Street, the distillery on Southside Street, and the Old Salt on the quay. Take your time; they've been waiting four hundred years.

else.text: {greeting} You're stood at the Mayflower Steps. In 1620 about a hundred people sailed from here for America. Families, mostly. Some for their faith, some for a fresh start.
I'm making a new display for the visitors. Would you gather the story for me? Three stops round the Barbican.

then.text: Lovely. Start at the Elizabethan House on New Street, then the gin distillery, then have a word with the Old Salt on the quay.

else.text: Fair enough. The Steps aren't going anywhere. They're steps.

then.text: Sixty-six days, and the Speedwell sold off for scrap. The Speedwell went back to London in disgrace. Never trust a ship called Speedwell. It's tempting fate.
The Mayflower didn't set out from here, you know. She sailed from Southampton with the Speedwell for company.
The Speedwell leaked like a basket. They put into Dartmouth to mend her, set off again, and she leaked again. So they came in here, to Plymouth, and left her behind.
Crammed everybody on to the Mayflower and went alone. Late in the year, mind. Autumn gales all the way. Brave, or daft. Usually both.
Go tell the historian. And tell her the Speedwell was a disgrace. She'll know what I mean.

else.text: Been on the water fifty years. Plymouth Sound is the best natural harbour in the world. I've seen two others and they didn't compare.

ply_janner.text: {greeting} You're not from round yer, are you? Plymouth folk are Janners. Nobody agrees why. I say it's because we're lovely.
If someone says they'll do it 'dreckly', that means some time, possibly never. 'Proper job' means well done. And 'where's it to?' means where is it. You'll pick it up, my 'ansum.

ply_matey.text: Devonport. The Navy's been building and mending ships here since 1691. There's submarines in there now, though I couldn't possibly comment.
Captain Scott was born just up the road, the one who went to the South Pole. And Darwin sailed on the Beagle from Plymouth Sound in 1831. Busy old Sound.

ply_swimmer.text: Tinside! Seawater pool, built in 1935, and all those lovely Art Deco curves. Bracing is the word. Blue is the colour.
On a good day you see seals off the Hoe, and once a whole pod of dolphins came right past the Breakwater. I screamed. They didn't seem to mind.

ply_gull.text: It looks pointedly at your bag, then at the pasty shop, then back at you. The message is clear.

ply_scott.text: I'm at the university here, studying marine biology. Plymouth's had a marine laboratory since 1888. Half my lectures are about plankton and I've never been happier.
Did you know Plymouth Sound and the estuaries round it are a special area of conservation? Seagrass, sea fans, the lot. It's a jungle down there. A wet one.

ply_blitz.text: My mum remembered the Blitz. Spring 1941, night after night. The whole middle of the city burned.
Charles Church was gutted and they left the shell standing as a memorial. And they say on the Hoe the people came up and danced, to show they weren't beaten. That's Plymouth for you.

ply_yardworker.text: Royal William Yard. Everything the Navy ate and drank came through here: biscuit from the bakery, beer from the brewery, salt beef from the slaughterhouse.
Over the gate there's a statue of King William IV. A whole yard of beautiful limestone and he's the one everybody photographs. Typical.

else.text: Is that a string of Roscoff onions? For me? My nan used to buy these off a Johnny on a bike every summer. Pink, sweet, lovely in a pasty. Thank you!

then.text: The Roscoff boat. About six hours across the Channel to Brittany: Breizh, where they speak a cousin of Cornish and Welsh.

else.text: The Roscoff boat's not taking foot passengers with creatures till you've a few more badges, I'm afraid. Insurance. Come back when you've got the Storm badge.
